claims.text: A gradient grain-size design introduced through multi-step forging or rolling under controlled strain will alleviate the strength-ductility trade-off in metallic alloys.
The alloy initially has a homogeneous microstructure.
Multi-step forging or rolling with controlled strain paths can create a surface-to-core grain-size gradient.
Moderate processing temperatures and incremental reductions allow partial recrystallization.
Moderate processing temperatures and incremental reductions enable controlled microstructural evolution.
The resulting gradient microstructure has refined grains near the surface and coarser grains in the interior.
Fine surface grains increase strength by impeding dislocation motion.
Coarser interior grains provide pathways for ductile deformation.
Combining fine surface grains with coarse interior grains balances strength and ductility.
Relative to uniformly processed material, the gradient-grained material will have higher yield strength or ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to uniformly processed material, the gradient-grained material will maintain or slightly improve ductility.
Homogeneous grain-size alloys generally exhibit an inverse relationship between strength and ductility under standard thermomechanical treatments.
The approach requires the alloy to form and retain distinct grain-size gradients without losing microstructural integrity.
Extremely high temperatures may reduce the effectiveness of the gradient-grain approach.
Extremely high strain rates may reduce the effectiveness of the gradient-grain approach.
The degree of strength and ductility improvement depends on alloy chemistry, deformation scheduling, and thermal history.
